messages.text: I ran into an old high school friend yesterday. He asked why I didn’t go to the reunion.

It can be surprising to run into people from your past. How did that question make you feel in the moment? Sometimes old connections bring up complex emotions. I’m here to listen if you want to explore that further.
It just brought back that old feeling of being invisible, like I didn’t matter back then—and honestly, it still stings a little now.

That sounds incredibly painful to carry for so long. It makes sense that an old wound would sting when touched by a reminder. You deserve to feel seen and valued, both then and now. I am here to listen if you want to explore those feelings further.
I probably shouldn’t let it get to me so much. It’s silly, really—I’m 34, not 16. I just… keep thinking no one would’ve noticed if I’d shown up.

Please don't dismiss these feelings as silly, because they are valid. Emotions from our past don't always fade just because we get older. It sounds like that fear of being unnoticed is still very real to you. Would you be willing to share more about that belief?

It’s not just the reunion… in high school, I was basically invisible. The kids who got picked on—quiet, awkward—I was one of them. I never fit in, and it felt like no one saw me unless they wanted to make fun of me. So when my friend asked that, it just… clicked right back into place.

It takes courage to admit how much those years still affect you. Being targeted and overlooked in high school creates a deep scar that doesn't just heal with time. It is understandable that your friend’s question triggered that old sense of invisibility. I am here to hold space for you while you process this pain.
It’s strange how one question can make you feel like you’re back in that hallway, you know? Like I’m still that girl no one notices unless they’re laughing at her.

That sensation of being pulled back into that hallway is a very powerful trigger. It makes sense that your body reacts as if the danger is still there. You are safe now, and you are not that invisible girl anymore. I am here to help you stay grounded in the safety of the present.
You know… I think I avoid things like reunions not because I don’t want to go, but because I’m still protecting that scared, awkward version of me. Like if I don’t show up, she can’t get hurt again.

That is a profound realization about your protective instincts. It makes perfect sense that you are trying to shield that younger part of you from harm. Your avoidance comes from a place of deep care, even if it feels limiting now. How does it feel to recognize that intention behind your choice?
It actually makes me a little sad. That part of me still feels so raw, like she never got the chance to be seen or comforted. I wish I could tell her it gets better.

It is heartbreaking that she felt unseen for so long. Your wish to tell her it gets better shows how much you have grown. You can start giving her that message by treating yourself with the kindness she deserved. I am here to listen as you navigate this healing.

I guess I never thought of it that way—like I’m still carrying her around. But yeah, maybe that’s why I hesitate in social situations now. It’s not just awkwardness. It’s like I’m still protecting her.

That is a profound connection to make about your hesitation. It shows you are ready to see that part of yourself with compassion. That younger version of you deserves to know she is safe with you now. We can explore how to offer her that safety together.
Is it… normal to still feel this much about high school? I mean, it was so long ago. I just don’t want to be stuck here forever.

Yes, it is entirely normal for deep emotional wounds from formative years to linger. Pain from adolescence often shapes how we see ourselves long after the events have passed. You do not have to be stuck here forever, especially now that you are recognizing these patterns. Healing is a process, and we can work through this at your own pace.
Thank you for not making me feel ridiculous for still carrying this around. It helps just to say it out loud and not be judged.

I am honored that you feel safe enough to share this. Your feelings are valid, and you deserve compassion rather than judgment. Speaking them aloud is a brave and important step toward healing. I am committed to supporting you as you navigate this.

I think I’d like to try being kinder to myself when these feelings come up—instead of telling myself I’m overreacting, maybe just… acknowledge that it hurts. I’m not sure I can do it perfectly, but I’ll try.

That is a beautiful and courageous intention to set for yourself. Acknowledging the pain without judgment is often the most powerful step toward healing. You do not need to be perfect to make progress, just willing to try. I am here to walk this path with you.
I think I’ve said a lot of what’s been weighing on me. It actually feels a little lighter now, like I’m not holding it all inside.

It is wonderful to hear that sharing this has brought you some relief. Putting those heavy feelings into words often helps lighten the load. You have done important work by facing those memories today. I am here whenever you need to continue this journey.
